title: How can we make good decisions?

paragraphs.text: In 1670, French philosopher Pascal wrote that, when faced with a choice, you should assess the positive or negative values of every outcome alongside each outcome's probability. Later, in 1738, mathematician Daniel Bernoulli noted two additional considerations — the decision-maker's attitude to risk, and the utility of a given payoff depending on their preferences or needs. For example, a small monetary gain would be of greater utility to a poor person than a rich person, and thus their decisions in the same gamble could be entirely different but equally sensible.

Historically, the science of decision-making was the province of economists, and their basic assumption was that people are essentially rational. The problem is we systematically make choices that go against what an economist would predict or advocate.

Then, in the 1970s, psychological scientists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky overturned these assumptions. One keystone of their theory is loss aversion, or the discovery that winning $100 is approximately half as appealing as losing $100 is unappealing. Another is the idea that the context and phrasing of a problem can influence a person's choice. In studies focusing on medical treatments, they showed that people seek a sure solution if a problem is phrased in terms of benefit, but accept risk when the problem is phrased in terms of potentially averting a negative outcome.

Real-world problems are often complicated, and our brains are naturally wired to use mental shortcuts called heuristics. One important heuristic is representativeness — the tendency to ignore statistics and focus on stereotypes. For example, someone is described as a helpful but shy and withdrawn man who loves structure and detail. When faced with a list of possible occupations including farmer and librarian, people tend to guess that he is a librarian because this fits a common stereotype. They ignore an obvious truth — there are many more farmers in the world than there are librarians.

People also assess the chance of an event occurring based on the ease with which it comes to mind, or its availability. For example, because dramatic events such as swimmers being attacked by sharks are frequently reported on TV and in the press, people invariably overestimate the probability of these rare outcomes. Another is the ‘affect heuristic’ — the tendency to assess probabilities based on how we feel towards particular options. Those feelings may not correspond to real-world risks. For example, people tend to fear radiation from nuclear power plants more than radiation from medical X-rays, yet it is actually X-rays that pose a greater risk to health.

Psychological scientists who study decision-making often draw a distinction between two types of mental processing. A fast, unconscious, often emotion-driven system that relies on personal experience, referred to as System 1, is contrasted with System 2, a slower, more analytical system that rationally balances benefits against costs. Both systems may be involved in making a choice, with System 2 monitoring the quality of the snap System 1 judgment and adjusting a decision accordingly. For experts in high-stakes domains, the 'gut reaction' of System 1 may lead to better real-world choices. In a study at Cornell University, expert cardiologists took fewer facts into account than younger doctors did when deciding whether to hospitalize emergency patients with chest pain. Experts also tended to process that information in an all-or-none fashion (a patient was either at risk of a heart attack or not) rather than wasting time dealing with shades of grey.

The fact that our gist-processing centers and our ability to use System 1 don't fully mature until our 20s may help explain the risky choices that younger decision-makers commonly make. Adolescents do risky things because their brains get bogged down in calculating odds. Youngsters are bombarded by warning statistics, yet risks of undesirable outcomes remain objectively small, and this may actually encourage young people to take those risks rather than avoid them. Adults, in contrast, make their choices more like expert doctors: making an immediate black-and-white judgment. They just say no to risky activities because, however objectively unlikely the risks, there's too much at stake to warrant even considering them.

So how can we help people make better decisions in the absence of immediate danger? System 2 is the obvious approach — analyze all known variables and quantify the different choices. This has significantly improved decisions in contexts such as academic admissions and hiring. Having decision-makers adopt an outsider's perspective on decisions can also reduce overconfidence in their knowledge. Considering multiple options simultaneously — as opposed to separately — can optimize outcomes and increase an individual's willpower in carrying out a choice. Decision-making by committee rather than individually can improve decisions in group contexts, as can making individuals more accountable for their decisions. Analogical reasoning can reduce System 1 errors by highlighting how a particular task shares underlying principles with another unrelated one, thereby helping people to see past surface details to more fully understand a problem.

In some domains, such as preventative healthcare, a better approach may be to work with, rather than against, our tendency to make gut System 1 decisions. Doctors and the media bombard patients with numerical data, and consumers tend to overestimate the risks involved. But when they learn their risk for a particular disease is lower than they initially thought, they become more complacent — for instance, by not undergoing screening. Instead, communicating the gist, 'You're at (some) risk; you should get screened because it detects disease early,' may be a more powerful motivator to make the right decision than the raw numbers would be.
